To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the subjective magnitude of rewarding brain stimulation varies as a function of the current and pulse frequency of the stimulation and also as a function of where the stimulation is delivered.

the subjective magnitude of stimulation reward is a nonlinear function of current, that the slope of this function is not the same for all sites of stimulation, and that the slope of the function is not a simple function of the fiber density at the site of stimulus application.

(1) the subjective magnitude of the rewarding effect of stimulation of the medial forebrain bundles is proportional to the logarithm of the stimulation current; and (2) the magnitude of the subjective growth in the rewarding effect of a given increase in stimulation current varies greatly between sites within the medial forebrain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how a brain stimulation reward is produced.
the question of whether the brain can be viewed as a system of spatio-temporal integrators of action potential barrages.
the relation between stimulation parameters and the subjective magnitude of stimulation reward.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the subjective magnitude of the reward produced by a given stimulus is a function of the site of stimulation, and the magnitude of the effect of the stimulation on the spatio-temporal pattern of activity in the medial forebrain-bundle reward-relevant fibers.
the subjective magnitude of stimulation reward varies with the site of stimulation because of differences between the spatio-temporal characteristics of the axons activated at different sites.

the magnitude of the subjective reward produced by electrical stimulation of the MFB is determined by the number and type of axons activated, the temporal distribution of the activity, and the spatial distribution of the activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the reward value of a stimulus is a function of the spatio- temporal pattern of action potentials in afferent fibers.

the medial fore-brain bundle terminates in more reward mechanisms than are usually recognized, each with a characteristic growth function relating the subjective reward magnitude to the stimulation strength, and each capable of being selectively excited by stimulation at a given site.
the medial fore brain bundle is not a single, unitary, spatio-temporaly integrating mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are multiple reward-relevant mechanisms, which differ in their sensitivity to stimulation strength, in the same brain area.
there are large differences in the subjective magnitude function between electrodes within one brain and between brains.
the reward value of brain stimulation varies greatly from one site to another, and that the variation is not readily explicable in terms of fiber density.
